_pages: Rendered sequence per lesson: setting → idea → apart → again → ext1 → ext2 … → watch → try. The Walkthrough pager (grammar-module.jsx ~3679, Session 14) already does paged-not-scrolled; this splits its single `watch` page into one page per extension and adds `setting` at the front.
_extensions: kind 'flip' = the same pattern from the LEARNER's side with a different object — this replaces the abstract `when` beat. kind 'wrinkle' = attaches to the module's own DEEP[point].wr[i] via the `wr` index; the wrinkle's teaching text stays in the module and is NOT copied here. kind 'extra' = a wrinkle the module does not have, so it carries its own `t`.
_register: Required, not merely observed (Lloyd, Session 17). The spine is the business a new resident cannot avoid: the residence card, the ward office, the fourteen-day deadline, the medical, the rules on the board.
_status: AI-AUTHORED, NOT REVIEWED. One batch per lesson. Three questions per lesson: are the claims true; is each line natural FOR ITS MOMENT; is this the pattern a Japanese speaker would reach for here.
_coverage: ALL NINE STAGES COMPLETE — every teaching point in Steps 0-33.

setting.scene: The immigration hall, after the flight and before the country starts. The officer takes your passport and the landing card you filled in somewhere over Siberia. If you are staying more than three months you will leave this desk holding a residence card — the document you are then required to carry every day you are here. He asks, in Japanese first, what you have come to do.
setting.jp: カードを見せます。
setting.en: Card show. — I show the card.

extensions.scene: An hour later, at the airport post office, you want a travel card for the trains. The words are not in your head yet, but the shape is, and the shape is the reverse of everything you have said out loud since you were two: whatever the thing is goes first, and whatever you are doing to it goes last.
extensions.jp: カードを買います。
extensions.en: Card buy. — I'll buy a card.

extensions.t: The last word decides everything — tense, politeness, question or statement, and whether the whole sentence was negative. English commits in the first three words; Japanese commits in the last two syllables, which is why you have to listen to the end of a sentence you thought you had already understood.
extensions.scene: The clerk answers with a sentence that begins exactly like the one you expected and then ends somewhere else entirely. Everything that mattered — whether it was a question, whether it was negative — arrived after you had already stopped listening.
extensions.jp: カードを買いますか。
extensions.en: Will you buy a card? — one syllable at the end, and it was a question all along.

claims: Residence cards are issued to foreign nationals staying more than three months
Carrying the card is a legal requirement for residents aged 16 and over
flags: STEP 0 LINES ARE ILLUSTRATIVE — 見せます and 買います are not taught yet. Step 0 exists to show sentence shape before any grammar, exactly as the module's own 'Coffee drink.' example does.

setting.scene: The ward office, second week, registering the address you must register inside fourteen days. The clerk has your form, your card and your passport laid out in front of her, so she already knows your name, your date of birth and where you now live. She looks up and asks what you do for a living, and there is exactly one piece of information in the room that she does not have.
setting.jp: 先生です。
setting.en: Teacher. — I'm a teacher.

extensions.scene: A fortnight later the school hands you a form of its own, and the teacher at the next desk reads the box over your shoulder and asks whether the person in the photo is your brother. He is not. Nothing in the answer needs to name him, or you, or the photograph.
extensions.jp: 友達です。
extensions.en: A friend. — He's a friend.

extensions.t: 私 does not disappear because it is impolite — it disappears because it is already known. Put it back in and you are drawing a contrast: 私は先生です answers 'and what about you?' rather than 'what do you do?'. That is why saying it in every sentence reads as strange rather than wrong.
extensions.scene: At the welcome lunch, everyone goes round the table. The person before you says what they do, and then it is your turn, and this is the one time all fortnight the word for I earns its place — because the sentence is not about you, it is about you as opposed to him.
extensions.jp: 私は先生です。
extensions.en: I'm a teacher — as opposed to whatever he just said.

claims: Address registration must be completed within 14 days of moving in

setting.scene: A police box, a Tuesday evening, and an officer has asked to see your card. The card is in your wallet, which is where it has to be — a photograph of it on your phone does not satisfy the law, and not carrying it is a fine of up to two hundred thousand yen. He reads the status printed on the front and asks, conversationally, what you are here for.
setting.jp: 学生です。
setting.en: I'm a student.

extensions.scene: Saturday, and a neighbour two doors down stops you by the bins to ask about the dog you have been walking, which is not yours — you are minding it for the family upstairs while they are away. One word and です does the whole job.
extensions.jp: 友達の犬です。
extensions.en: It's a friend's dog.

extensions.scene: Later the same conversation she asks whether the vet was expensive, and the answer needs an adjective rather than a noun. です comes along anyway, and this time it is carrying nothing but manners.
extensions.jp: 高いです。
extensions.en: It's expensive — です adds politeness, nothing else.

claims: Police may ask foreign residents to produce their residence card; failure to carry it is punishable by a fine of up to ¥200,000
A photocopy or phone photograph does not satisfy the requirement
flags: How routine such stops are varies by area and is contested; the setting says 'has asked' without claiming a frequency.

setting.scene: The counter at the city office, and three things are on it: the form you have just filled in, in front of you; your residence card, which the clerk has slid to her side to copy the number off; and a rack of leaflets against the far wall that you will need one of before you leave. She asks which of them is yours to take away.
setting.jp: それはカードです。
setting.en: That one — by you — is the card.

extensions.scene: Now you are the one asking. The leaflet you need is behind her on the rack, out of reach of both of you, and pointing at it is the entire sentence — the word you choose says how far away it is from the pair of you.
extensions.jp: あれをください。
extensions.en: That one over there, please.

extensions.scene: Somebody comes to the counter and speaks to the clerk by name, and you want to know who he is. He is not near you and not near her. The far word does the work again, and this time the thing it points at is a person.
extensions.jp: あの人は誰ですか。
extensions.en: Who is that person over there?

flags: No factual claims — an ordinary situation.

setting.scene: The station lost-property window, the morning after you left a bag on the train. The man behind the counter goes into the back and returns with three of them, which he sets on a shelf well out of reach of either of you. He does not ask you to describe it. He waits for you to point, and the choice is not one decision but two.
setting.jp: あれです。
setting.en: That one — away from us both.

extensions.scene: He brings it down and asks whether the umbrella hooked on the strap is yours too. It is now in his hands, a metre from your face — which by the rule you have just learned is not near you at all, whatever the tape measure says.
extensions.jp: それも私のです。
extensions.en: That one's mine too.

extensions.t: The second decision is which set. これ・それ・あれ stand alone in place of a noun; この・その・あの cannot stand at all and must be holding one. これ本です is the error the two sets produce, and it is the commonest in this step.
extensions.scene: He asks you to sign for it, and the form wants the item written in — so now the pointing word has a noun to hold, and the word itself has to change to hold it.
extensions.jp: そのかばんです。
extensions.en: That bag — pointing word plus noun, so それ becomes その.

flags: No factual claims — an ordinary situation.

setting.scene: The clerk has been working from your visa category and has ticked the box that says student. You are not one — you are here to work, and that box decides which of two forms you spend the next twenty minutes on. Her hand is already going to the wrong pile, and you have about four seconds and one sentence.
setting.jp: 学生じゃないです。
setting.en: I'm not a student.

extensions.scene: A week later, at the school gate, a parent takes you for the other foreign teacher — the one who left in March. Same shape, different noun, and it is the politest available way to stop a conversation going somewhere neither of you wants.
extensions.jp: 日本人じゃないです。
extensions.en: I'm not Japanese.

extensions.scene: She apologises and asks whether the textbook you are holding was expensive, meaning to be kind about it. It was not — and the word for expensive refuses this negative entirely, because it is not a noun and it can do the job itself.
extensions.jp: この本は高くないです。
extensions.en: This book is not expensive — the adjective negates itself.

claims: The status of residence printed on the card determines which procedures apply

setting.scene: You took the afternoon off, cycled twenty minutes and found the shutters down. Municipal offices keep short weekday hours and shut at weekends, so the errand you have to complete inside fourteen days now has eleven left in it. The next morning somebody at work asks whether you got it sorted.
setting.jp: 休みでした。
setting.en: It was closed.

extensions.scene: She asks whether the ride over was at least pleasant, which it was not — it rained the whole way there and stopped the moment you turned round. Same past tense, your sentence this time, and the word in front of it is a noun again.
extensions.jp: 雨でした。
extensions.en: It was rain. — It was raining.

extensions.scene: You want to add that it was not raining on the way back, which needs the past and the negative at once. Nothing new is required: two pieces you already own, stacked in that order.
extensions.jp: 昨日は雨じゃなかったです。
extensions.en: Yesterday it wasn't rainy.

extensions.scene: What you actually want to say is that it was cold, and that is where the sentence breaks — because cold is not a noun, and it will not accept でした at any price. It carries its own past inside itself.
extensions.jp: 昨日は寒かったです。
extensions.en: Yesterday was cold — the adjective changed shape.

claims: Municipal offices generally keep weekday daytime hours and close at weekends
The 14-day registration deadline runs regardless of whether the office was open
flags: Some municipalities run limited evening or Saturday counters; the setting does not claim otherwise.

setting.scene: Four windows, four queues, and a numbered ticket in your hand that does not say which of them it belongs to. The signs above each one are in kanji you cannot read yet. Everybody in the room knows where they are going except you, and the only tool you have is a sentence you can already say with one sound added to the end.
setting.jp: これですか。
setting.en: Is it this one?

extensions.scene: It was not that one. At the right window the clerk hands you a second form, and now you are asking whether this is the last of them — the same one syllable, doing the same work, on a sentence you built yourself.
extensions.jp: これは最後ですか。
extensions.en: Is this the last one?

extensions.scene: The teacher next to you at lunch asks the same kind of question and it sounds nothing like yours: no か at all, just the pitch going up at the end. Written down, meanwhile, the question you asked at the counter would end with a full stop.
extensions.jp: 学生？
extensions.en: Student? — casual: か drops, the pitch does the work.

flags: No factual claims — an ordinary situation.
最後 uses 後, outside KANJI_DICT — furigana needed, or swap the sentence.

setting.scene: The immigration office, renewing your status. The officer is reading from your file and confirming one detail he already believes he knows. 「学生じゃないですか」 — you're not a student, are you? You are not. Your English instinct is about to answer the fact, and the fact is no, so the word arriving in your mouth is the wrong one.
setting.jp: はい、学生じゃないです。
setting.en: That's right — I'm not a student.

extensions.scene: Later that week you are the one asking. The neighbour has not put her bins out and you want to check she is not away — and the question you build is a negative one, which means her はい will mean yes-you're-right-I'm-not.
extensions.jp: 明日、いませんか。
extensions.en: You won't be here tomorrow?

extensions.t: The escape while the reflex builds: drop the particle and answer with the predicate. 学生じゃないですか — 学生です。 No はい, no いいえ, nothing to get backwards, and native speakers do it constantly for exactly the same reason.
extensions.scene: The officer asks a second one and you can feel yourself computing. So you skip the yes-or-no entirely and say the fact, which is shorter, completely natural, and impossible to get the wrong way round.
extensions.jp: 学生です。
extensions.en: I'm a student. — answering the fact, not the phrasing.

claims: Negative questions are common in polite Japanese because they soften the asking
flags: The softening claim is the module's own teaching; it is linguistic judgement rather than a sourced fact.

setting.scene: A form with eleven boxes, of which you have confidently filled in three. The clerk has stepped away. The man beside you is filling in the same form at speed, and you need to know what goes in the fourth box badly enough to interrupt him — with a finger on it, so the question has somewhere to land.
setting.jp: これは何ですか。
setting.en: What is this?

extensions.scene: He tells you, and then the next box needs a different question — not what it is but where the thing goes. The word changes and nothing else in the sentence moves, which is the whole trick and takes about a week to trust.
extensions.jp: どこですか。
extensions.en: Where is it?

extensions.scene: A name gets called twice and nobody stands up, and you ask the man beside you who it was. The question word lands in the subject's seat — and that seat, when a question word is sitting in it, never takes は.
extensions.jp: 誰が来ましたか。
extensions.en: Who came? — 誰が, never 誰は.

flags: No factual claims — an ordinary situation.

setting.scene: Forty minutes into a numbered wait at the city office, on a row of plastic chairs, beside a woman who arrived before you did. Neither of you is going anywhere. She catches your eye and says something about the weather — and what she is doing is not conveying information, because you are both sitting in the same room and you both already know it.
setting.jp: いい天気ですね。
setting.en: Nice weather, isn't it.

extensions.scene: Your number is two away and hers is next, and the wait has been long enough that saying so out loud is a small act of solidarity rather than a complaint. You go first this time.
extensions.jp: 長いですね。
extensions.en: It's long, isn't it.

extensions.scene: Then you nearly tell her something she cannot possibly know — that the counter shuts at five — with the same ね on the end, and it comes out wrong, because there is nothing there for her to agree with.
extensions.jp: 五時までですね。
extensions.en: It's until five, isn't it — only works if she already knew.

flags: No factual claims — an ordinary situation.
長い and 五時 sit slightly ahead of the Step 1 bank; both appear in module examples by Step 3.

setting.scene: The same waiting room, a week later. A man two seats along is holding the pale blue form, and you know from getting it wrong yourself last Tuesday that the counter he is queuing for wants the white one. He is about to stand up. You have one short sentence and no vocabulary for any of the nouns involved.
setting.jp: それじゃないですよ。
setting.en: That's not the one, you know.

extensions.scene: He thanks you and asks where the white ones are kept, and you know that too, because you have been here three times this month. Genuine news, delivered by you, to someone who did not have it: the same particle, doing the same job.
extensions.jp: あそこにありますよ。
extensions.en: They're over there, you know.

extensions.scene: What you are less sure about is whether the counter takes cards, and you want to say so in a way that states your belief and asks him to confirm it. Both particles stack, in that order, and only that order.
extensions.jp: この店は安いですよね。
extensions.en: This shop's cheap, right? — stating and checking at once.

flags: No factual claims — an ordinary situation.

setting.scene: August, no air conditioning worth the name in the older part of the building, and an hour on the plastic chairs. The woman beside you has been there as long as you have. The clerk who comes out to call the next number has spent the morning behind a desk in the cooled office at the back, and says the same thing about the heat that everyone has been saying all morning.
setting.jp: 暑いですね。
setting.en: Hot, isn't it — we both feel it.

extensions.scene: You say it back to the clerk as she passes, and it is the wrong particle for her — she has just come out of the cool room and has not been in this since eight. What she needs is the news setting, not the agreement one.
extensions.jp: 暑いですよ。
extensions.en: It's hot out here — you haven't been in it.

extensions.t: The mistake that lands worst is よ about the listener's own experience. 疲れていますよ tells someone how tired they are, which is exactly as presumptuous in Japanese as it sounds in English. When unsure: ね if you are sharing, nothing at all if you are not.
extensions.scene: An hour later you nearly tell the woman beside you that she must be tired, with よ on the end, and stop — because the one thing you cannot deliver as news is how somebody else feels.
extensions.jp: 疲れましたね。
extensions.en: You must be tired — shared, not announced.

flags: No factual claims — an ordinary situation.

setting.scene: The bank, opening an account, which needs the card and the address you registered a fortnight ago. The teller is working down a list, and each question puts a different thing on the table — your address, your employer, your reason for opening it. Then she reaches the line about you, and pauses with the pen over it.
setting.jp: 私は学生です。
setting.en: As for me — student.

extensions.scene: Two questions later she moves the conversation onto the account itself, and you follow her — because は does not mean I, it means here is the thing we are now discussing, and the thing you are discussing has just changed.
extensions.jp: この口座は新しいです。
extensions.en: This account is new.

extensions.scene: You read the form back to yourself under your breath and it does not sound like it is spelled. The character you have been writing all morning is not making the sound it makes anywhere else in the language.
extensions.jp: 私は学生です。
extensions.en: Read watashi WA — は as a particle is pronounced wa.

claims: Opening a bank account generally requires a residence card and a registered address
flags: 口座 uses kanji outside KANJI_DICT — furigana needed, or swap for a simpler noun.

setting.scene: Your number is called and you stand, and so does somebody else — a friend has come along to help with the Japanese, and the clerk has never met them and has no idea who they are. She looks between the two of you. What the sentence has to do is put a person into the conversation who was not in it a second ago.
setting.jp: 友達が来ました。
setting.en: A friend came with me.

extensions.scene: Walking home you pass the park and there is a dog loose by the gate with no one anywhere near it. Same job, different thing arriving: nobody knew the dog was there until you said so.
extensions.jp: 公園に犬がいます。
extensions.en: There's a dog in the park.

extensions.scene: Your friend asks whether you understood any of what the clerk said at the end. Some words never negotiate about this particle — understanding is one of them, and it takes が whether or not anything is arriving.
extensions.jp: 日本語がわかります。
extensions.en: I understand Japanese — わかる always takes が.

flags: No factual claims — an ordinary situation.

setting.scene: The clerk has understood that somebody came with you and now wants to know what they are to you, which is a second question about a person who has stopped being a surprise. The same human being is about to appear in two consecutive sentences, and the particle changes between them for a reason English has no word for.
setting.jp: 友達が来ました。友達は日本人です。
setting.en: A friend came. The friend is Japanese.

extensions.scene: That evening you tell the story to someone else and do the same handoff without thinking about it — the cat that turned up on the balcony arrives new, and by the second sentence it is a cat you are both discussing.
extensions.jp: 猫が来ました。その猫は小さかったです。
extensions.en: A cat came. The cat was small.

extensions.t: The question test settles most cases in a second. If the sentence answers which one, it takes が — and so does the question that asked it. If it just names what you are already talking about, it takes は.
extensions.scene: At the school gate the next morning somebody asks who was at the office with you. The question and the answer both point at a person out of a set of possible people, so both of them take the same particle.
extensions.jp: 誰が来ましたか。— 友達が来ました。
extensions.en: Who came? — A friend did.

flags: No factual claims — an ordinary situation.

setting.scene: The counter opens at half past eight and the queue starts before it. You have set an alarm for the first time since you arrived and you are eating standing up, because the difference between arriving at twenty-five past and arriving at ten to nine is about ninety minutes of your day. Everything in the sentence is ordinary; the particle is the whole lesson.
setting.jp: 朝ごはんを食べます。
setting.en: I eat breakfast.

extensions.scene: On the way you stop at the bakery by the station, because the queue will be long and there is nothing to do in it. Different verb, different object, same tag on the thing the action lands on.
extensions.jp: パンを買います。
extensions.en: I buy bread.

extensions.scene: Waiting, you try to say that you like the bakery — and the sentence refuses the particle you have just learned. Liking is not something you do to a bakery; the grammar treats it as a state, and states take a different marker.
extensions.jp: この店が好きです。
extensions.en: I like this shop — 好き takes が, not を.

flags: No factual claims — an ordinary situation.

setting.scene: You have been putting the ward office off for nine days and there are five left. Somebody at work asks when you are finally going to go, and the honest answer is the one you have been avoiding — not next week, not on some numbered day you could write in a diary, but today, straight after this conversation.
setting.jp: 今日、行きます。
setting.en: I'm going today.

extensions.scene: She asks what time, and the answer is now a number on a clock — which is precisely the kind of time that does take the particle you just left out of the sentence before it. Both rules, one after the other, thirty seconds apart.
extensions.jp: 七時に行きます。
extensions.en: I'm going at seven.

extensions.scene: Getting there before it shuts means getting up earlier, every day, for the rest of the week — and that sentence needs both kinds of time at once, one bare and one marked.
extensions.jp: 毎日七時に起きます。
extensions.en: Every day (bare) at seven (に) I get up.

flags: No factual claims — an ordinary situation.
No error-contrast: the design bans one in Steps 0-2, so 今日に行きます is named in the module's own watch beat rather than shown here.

setting.scene: Public libraries are free to people who live in the area and the card takes about ten minutes, provided you can prove you live where you say you live — which is the same piece of paper everything else has wanted this month. It is the first errand of the fortnight nobody is making you do.
setting.jp: 図書館に行きます。
setting.en: I'm going to the library.

extensions.scene: The librarian asks, making conversation, where you came from — meaning the country, and meaning the journey rather than the place. The other destination particle is a shade softer and does the same job.
extensions.jp: 日本へ来ました。
extensions.en: I came to Japan.

extensions.scene: You want to add that you will study there, and the sentence takes a different particle for the same building — because you have stopped talking about going and started talking about doing.
extensions.jp: 図書館で勉強します。
extensions.en: I study at the library — arriving is に, doing is で.

claims: Public library membership is generally free to residents of the municipality and requires proof of address
flags: UNSOURCED: library card requirements are municipal and vary. Stated loosely for that reason; confirm before shipping.

setting.scene: An online application, in Japanese, that will not let you past the name field. You have switched the keyboard over and you are typing what you hear, which is how わたしわ has now gone into the box twice. What is on the screen is not what the sentence sounds like, and the two have to be told apart before anything else will work.
setting.jp: 私は学校へ行きます。
setting.en: Read: watashi wa gakkou e ikimasu — two spelling quirks in one short sentence.

extensions.scene: You get past it and hit the same wall one field later, on the box that wants what you are applying for. The third quirky particle is the easy one — it exists for nothing except this job, so it is always the same sound.
extensions.jp: 本を買います。
extensions.en: I'm buying a book — を is typed 'wo' and read o.

extensions.t: One sentence can carry the same kana both ways. はなはきれいです — the first は belongs to the flower, the second is the particle. Reading aloud is where this shows up; typing わたしわ is how it shows up in the other direction.
extensions.scene: The form's example line has the same character in it twice, and only one of them changes its sound. Nothing marks which is which except what each one is doing.
extensions.jp: はなはきれいです。
extensions.en: Flowers are pretty — first は is hana, second is the particle wa.

flags: No factual claims — an ordinary situation.
The gloss contains romaji, normally banned outside the kana module. Deliberate: this lesson IS the sound-spelling mismatch and cannot be taught without naming both.

setting.scene: Your apartment has one room and a wall shared with somebody who works nights. The park by the station has benches, and on Saturday mornings a man practises a wind instrument at the far end of it, which somehow makes concentrating easier rather than harder. You have arranged to meet the friend who came to the ward office with you.
setting.jp: 公園で友達に会いました。
setting.en: I met a friend at the park.

extensions.scene: It rains, so you move to the library, and the sentence follows you without changing shape — the particle marks wherever the doing happens, and the doing has just moved indoors.
extensions.jp: 図書館で勉強します。
extensions.en: I study at the library.

extensions.scene: You want to say the books you need are in there, and the sentence quietly refuses — because nothing is happening in it. Sitting on a shelf is not an action, and a place where nothing is being done takes the other particle.
extensions.jp: 図書館に本があります。
extensions.en: There are books in the library — existing, not doing.

flags: No factual claims — an ordinary situation.

setting.scene: The ward office is two stations away. You have no car — that would mean proving to the police you have somewhere off-street to keep it — and the bicycle a departing colleague left you is still not registered in your name. So every errand this month has started on the same platform, and the sentence for it marks the train as a tool rather than a place.
setting.jp: 電車で行きます。
setting.en: I'll go by train.

extensions.scene: At the counter you cannot follow the clerk's question and ask her to use the other language, which is the same particle again — not a vehicle this time but a medium, which the grammar treats identically.
extensions.jp: 日本語で話します。
extensions.en: Let's speak in Japanese.

extensions.scene: Going home you decide to walk it, and the one everyday method that refuses this particle is the one you are using. Walking gets a verb form instead, which arrives properly in Step 4.
extensions.jp: 駅まで歩いて行きます。
extensions.en: I'll walk to the station — 歩いて, never 歩きで.

claims: Registering a car requires a police-issued parking certificate (車庫証明) under the 1962 Garage Act
flags: Bicycle registration (防犯登録) is mentioned in passing and not sourced; it is near-universal in practice but the requirement is prefectural.

setting.scene: The library card worked. You are in there on a Sunday for the second time and you want to say two things about the same building: that you come here to work, and that the thing you are looking for is somewhere on the second floor. The room does not change between those two sentences. The particle does.
setting.jp: 図書館に本があります。
setting.en: There are books in the library — existence.

extensions.scene: The librarian asks what you are doing up there every weekend, and the answer is about an action rather than a location. Same building, same shelves, third sentence in a row about them — and the particle flips back, because the verb changed.
extensions.jp: 二階で勉強します。
extensions.en: I study on the second floor.

extensions.t: Ask one question before choosing and it comes out right every time: is something happening here, or is something simply located here? Happening takes で. Located takes に. The place never decides — the verb does.
extensions.scene: Both of your sentences were about the same shelves on the same floor of the same building, and nothing about the room had anything to do with which particle each one wanted. The verb decided both times, and the verb was the only thing that changed.
extensions.jp: 公園で会います。公園に犬がいます。
extensions.en: We meet at the park. There's a dog in the park.

flags: No factual claims — an ordinary situation.
二階 uses 階, outside KANJI_DICT — furigana needed.

setting.scene: First proper shop after the arrival week, and you are buying for an empty kitchen. The list in your hand has two things on it because two things is what will fit in the basket alongside the rice you already have. At the till the assistant asks whether that is everything, and it is — exactly that, nothing else.
setting.jp: パンと牛乳を買いました。
setting.en: I bought bread and milk.

extensions.scene: On the way out you meet the teacher from the next desk, who asks who you came with. The same particle does a second job that English splits off into a different word entirely — joining things, and naming the person you are with.
extensions.jp: 友達と行きました。
extensions.en: I went with a friend.

extensions.scene: She asks what else is in the fridge and you start listing, and this is where と stops being the right tool — because it claims the list is finished, and yours is a sample of a fridge you have not properly looked in.
extensions.jp: 肉や魚があります。
extensions.en: There's meat and fish and so on — や, not と.

flags: No factual claims — an ordinary situation.

setting.scene: The staffroom, the first week of term, and the introductions have been going round the table for ten minutes. The person before you has just said which school they came from, and it happens to be the same one you were at last year in a different country — a coincidence worth one sentence and not more.
setting.jp: 私も学生です。
setting.en: I'm a student too.

extensions.scene: Later somebody asks whether anyone else is free on Monday and two hands go up including yours. The particle attaches to whatever is being added, and this time what is being added is a day.
extensions.jp: 月曜日も行きます。
extensions.en: I'm going on Monday as well.

extensions.scene: You try to say it about yourself with the topic particle still attached and the sentence will not take both. This one arrives and evicts whatever was standing there — it does not stack.
extensions.jp: 私も行きます。
extensions.en: I'm going too — も replaces は, never joins it.

flags: No factual claims — an ordinary situation.

setting.scene: Somebody has left a textbook on the shared desk and nobody has claimed it for three days. It has your surname written inside the cover in roman letters, which is either a coincidence or the school office being efficient about the order you put in a fortnight ago. The teacher beside you picks it up and holds it out, eyebrows raised.
setting.jp: 私の本です。
setting.en: It's my book.

extensions.scene: You hand back a different one that has been sitting under it, because that one is hers — same glue, other direction, and the owner always comes first while the thing owned comes last.
extensions.jp: 先生の本です。
extensions.en: It's the teacher's book.

extensions.scene: A third book turns up belonging to the teacher who teaches you Japanese on Wednesdays, and now the chain has three links in it. Read from the right and it unwinds cleanly; read from the left and it makes no sense at all.
extensions.jp: 私の日本語の先生の本です。
extensions.en: My Japanese teacher's book — the LAST noun is the thing.

flags: No factual claims — an ordinary situation.

setting.scene: The stationery order form has a column you cannot parse, because every line on it is three nouns stuck together with the same character and no clue about which one is the item. It is the commonest particle on the page and it is doing a different job in almost every row.
setting.jp: 私の日本語の先生の本です。
setting.en: Chains unwind from the right: my Japanese teacher's book.

extensions.scene: You fill in your own line and the same particle does a job that is not possession at all — it names where something is from, which English would need a whole preposition for.
extensions.jp: 日本の本です。
extensions.en: It's a Japanese book — origin, not ownership.

extensions.t: The classic overreach: の does NOT attach describing-words to nouns. きれいの人 is wrong — words like きれい bring their own connector (きれいな人), and words like 高い attach directly (高い店). If both sides are not nouns, this is not the particle you want.
extensions.scene: You try to write pretty notebook in the description column, reach for the particle that has worked all morning, and produce something that is not a phrase in any register of the language.
extensions.jp: きれいなノートです。
extensions.en: A pretty notebook — きれい brings its own な.

flags: No factual claims — an ordinary situation.
ノート is katakana and unlisted; harmless, but flagging the vocabulary reach.

setting.scene: You have been in the country a month and somebody who read your self-introduction says, kindly, that it sounded a little stiff. Reading it back, every sentence starts the same way — the word for I, eleven times in nine lines, because that is what English taught your hands to do.
setting.jp: 昨日映画を見ました。とても面白かったです。
setting.en: No 私 anywhere — and completely natural.

extensions.scene: You rewrite it. The one place the word stays is the line where you are being contrasted with the teacher who left — because there the sentence is genuinely about which of the two of you is meant.
extensions.jp: 私は先生です。
extensions.en: I'M the teacher — contrast, so 私 earns its place.

extensions.t: あなた is not the fix. Toward someone whose name you know it reads as cold or confrontational, whatever the textbook says. The word English uses for you is done in Japanese with the person's name plus さん — 田中さんは — which is what あなた's job actually is.
extensions.scene: You try to ask the teacher beside you what she thinks, reach for the word every phrasebook gives for you, and get a small pause in return. Her name has been on the desk sign the whole time.
extensions.jp: 田中さんはどう思いますか。
extensions.en: What do you think? — the name, not あなた.

flags: No factual claims — an ordinary situation.
思う arrives in Step 12; used here as a fixed phrase.

setting.scene: The ward office notice is four lines long and two of them are numbers. You have been caught out once already by turning up at the wrong end of the afternoon, and the counter you need has different hours from the rest of the building. The pair of particles on that line is the whole message.
setting.jp: 九時から五時まで働きます。
setting.en: Open from nine to five.

extensions.scene: You tell the school office when you are around on Thursdays, and it is the same pair doing the same work on your own timetable — a start, an end, and nothing needed in between.
extensions.jp: 月曜日から金曜日まで学校にいます。
extensions.en: I'm at school Monday to Friday.

extensions.t: から has a second life meaning because, arriving in Step 11. Position tells you which is which: after a noun it is from; after a whole clause it is because. Same word, two stations.
extensions.scene: Halfway down the same notice the character turns up again, and this time nothing in front of it is a place or a time — it is a whole sentence, and the meaning has quietly changed underneath you.
extensions.jp: 休みですから、行きません。
extensions.en: It's closed, so I'm not going — から after a clause is because.

flags: No factual claims — an ordinary situation.
金曜日 uses 金, outside KANJI_DICT — furigana needed.

setting.scene: Two apartments, both within cycling distance of the school, and you have to tell the agent which one by Friday. One is cheaper and forty minutes from the station; the other is neither. Everybody who asks wants the comparison in one sentence, and the sentence puts the two things in an order English would reverse.
setting.jp: この家はあの家より安いです。
setting.en: This place is cheaper than that one.

extensions.scene: The agent asks it back the other way round, about the commute rather than the rent, so you rebuild it with the other option as the yardstick — because より attaches to the thing being measured against, not to the thing being measured.
extensions.jp: バスは電車より安いです。
extensions.en: The bus is cheaper than the train.

extensions.scene: You listen for the word to change the way English changes cheap into cheaper, and it never does. The adjective stands exactly as it is and the particle carries the entire comparison on its own.
extensions.jp: 犬は猫より大きいです。
extensions.en: The dog is bigger than the cat — 大きい never inflects.

flags: No factual claims — an ordinary situation.
速い and 家 sit at the edge of the Step 3 bank; 家 is in it, 速い is not.

setting.scene: The school lunch order form wants a choice for each day of the coming month, and the two options are printed side by side with a single character between them. It is a character you have seen at the end of every question you have asked since your first week, and it is not doing that job here.
setting.jp: コーヒーかお茶を飲みます。
setting.en: I'll drink coffee or tea.

extensions.scene: The office asks which day suits for the medical, and you genuinely do not mind, so you hand the choice back — the same character, between two days instead of two drinks.
extensions.jp: 月曜日か火曜日がいいです。
extensions.en: Monday or Tuesday would be good.

extensions.scene: Your reply ends up with the character twice in one line, once in the middle and once at the very end, and they are not the same word doing two jobs so much as two words sharing a shape. Where it sits tells you which.
extensions.jp: 月曜日か火曜日ですか。
extensions.en: Is it Monday or Tuesday? — middle か is 'or', final か asks.

flags: No factual claims — an ordinary situation.
火曜日 uses 火, outside KANJI_DICT — furigana needed.

setting.scene: The neighbour who has been signing for your parcels asks what you have got in for the week, and the honest answer is that you do not entirely know — you shopped fast and put things away faster. What you can give her is a couple of examples and the clear signal that the list is not the whole of it.
setting.jp: 肉や魚があります。
setting.en: There's meat and fish and that sort of thing.

extensions.scene: She asks what is on the desk you have been complaining about, and the same word does the same job: two examples out of a surface you would rather not inventory.
extensions.jp: 机の上に本やペンがあります。
extensions.en: There are books, pens and so on on the desk.

extensions.scene: Say it with the other joining particle instead and you have claimed to have counted — that the fridge holds meat and fish and nothing whatever besides, which is a strange thing to be certain about.
extensions.jp: 肉と魚があります。
extensions.en: There's meat and fish — と says that's the complete list.

flags: No factual claims — an ordinary situation.
机 and ペン sit outside the Step 3 bank; both appear in the module's own example for this point.

setting.scene: A medical for the job, and the instruction sheet says nothing from midnight. At half past seven the nurse asks whether you have had anything this morning, and you have — one glass of water, because the sheet said nothing about water and you were not going to guess. The answer is a plain statement of a limit, with no feeling attached to it.
setting.jp: 水だけ飲みます。
setting.en: I only drink water.

extensions.scene: She asks how long you have been in the country and the answer is short enough to want the same word — a flat limit, stated without apology, which is exactly what this particle is for.
extensions.jp: 一か月だけです。
extensions.en: Only a month.

extensions.scene: There is another word for only, one lesson away, and it means the same fact with a sigh attached. Choosing between them is choosing whether the limit is neutral or disappointing.
extensions.jp: 水しか飲みません。
extensions.en: I've only got water — しか adds the sigh だけ doesn't.

flags: No factual claims — an ordinary situation.
一か月 uses 月 in a counter reading; furigana decision needed.

setting.scene: The last bus has gone. There is a taxi rank with no taxi on it and one shop still lit. Cashless payment reached 42.8% of consumer spending in 2024 against a government target of 80%, and out here that average means nothing — the shop takes cash, the taxi firm takes cash, and you are counting what is in your wallet before you go in.
setting.jp: 千円しかありません。
setting.en: I've only got a thousand yen.

extensions.scene: The shopkeeper phones a driver anyway and asks how much you have. You say it again to a second person, and it is still the version with the sigh in it, because the amount is still not enough.
extensions.jp: 百円しかありません。
extensions.en: I've only got a hundred yen.

extensions.scene: Written out, the sentence looks like it should mean you have no money at all — the verb is negative and the meaning is not. It is one of the few patterns where trusting the shape beats translating the parts.
extensions.jp: 百円しかありません。
extensions.en: I have only 100 yen — negative verb, positive meaning.

claims: Cashless payments reached 42.8% of consumer spending in 2024 (METI)
Japan's long-term cashless target is 80%, with 65% by 2030
flags: The rural cash-only detail is resident experience rather than a sourced statistic; the national figure is sourced, the local inference is not.

setting.scene: A greengrocer with everything in open boxes and no barcodes, which means saying out loud how many you want rather than putting them in a basket and letting a machine work it out. There are four people behind you. The number is the easy part; the word that has to follow it is not.
setting.jp: りんごを三つ買いました。
setting.en: I bought three apples.

extensions.scene: At the counter next door you order for two, which needs the counter for people — and that one has irregular readings in exactly the places you will need most often.
extensions.jp: 二人です。
extensions.en: Two people — read ふたり, not におん.

extensions.scene: You try to put the number in front of the fruit the way English does and the sentence comes apart. The count does not glue to the noun; it floats along behind the particle, just in front of the verb.
extensions.jp: りんごを三つ買いました。
extensions.en: Never 三つりんごを — the count floats after the particle.

flags: No factual claims — an ordinary situation.

setting.scene: small izakaya on a Friday with the whole section, and you have been sent to the counter to order for the table. Two beers is a sentence you have practised. It comes out fine. Three of them, twenty minutes later, does not — because the number and the counter change each other's sound when they meet.
setting.jp: ビールを二本ください。
setting.en: Two beers, please — 二本 stays plain: にほん.

extensions.scene: The second round is three, and the word you practised has quietly changed shape in your mouth. Nothing about the writing warned you; this is a sound rule, learned by ear and drilled as a chant.
extensions.jp: ビールを三本ください。
extensions.en: Three beers — さんぼん, not さんほん.

extensions.t: Priorities, because there are dozens of counters and you do not need them. ひとり and ふたり are non-negotiable. The 〜本 row is the classic shift set. Past that, relax — a wrong counter is understood and gently corrected, while a MISSING one is genuinely broken.
extensions.scene: Somebody asks for something you have no counter for at all, and uses the all-purpose one instead, and nothing whatever goes wrong. That is the escape hatch, and it is always a sentence.
extensions.jp: みっつください。
extensions.en: Three, please — 〜つ rescues almost anything.

flags: No factual claims — an ordinary situation.
No factual claims — an ordinary situation.

setting.scene: The school wants to know how long your commute is, for the paperwork that decides your travel allowance. You have done it eleven times and it has never taken the same number of minutes twice. The form has a box for a number and no box for it depends, so the sentence needs a way to say roughly.
setting.jp: 三十分ぐらいかかります。
setting.en: It takes about thirty minutes.

extensions.scene: The same form asks how much you spend on it a month, and the answer is another number you cannot pin down. The same word fuzzes an amount of money exactly as it fuzzed an amount of time.
extensions.jp: 一万円ぐらいです。
extensions.en: About ten thousand yen.

extensions.scene: The next box wants what time you leave the house, and reaching for the same word puts a smear across a point on the clock rather than across a length. There is a different word for that, and it is the next lesson.
extensions.jp: 七時ごろ出ます。
extensions.en: I leave around seven — a point in time takes ごろ.

flags: No factual claims — an ordinary situation.
一万円 uses 万, outside KANJI_DICT — furigana needed.

setting.scene: The neighbour who signs for your parcels wants to know when you are usually back, so she knows when it is worth ringing the bell rather than leaving a card. You are back at about the same time every day and at exactly that time on no day at all, and she is asking about a point on the clock rather than a length of anything.
setting.jp: 七時ごろ帰ります。
setting.en: I get home around seven.

extensions.scene: You ask her the same thing back, because there is a parcel of hers you have taken in twice, and the question uses the same word about the same kind of time.
extensions.jp: 何時ごろですか。
extensions.en: About what time?

extensions.scene: You write it down for her with the time particle in as well, out of habit, and it is one piece too many — this word has already done that job on its way past.
extensions.jp: 七時ごろ帰ります。
extensions.en: No に needed — ごろ replaces it rather than joining it.

flags: No factual claims — an ordinary situation.

setting.scene: You write three sentences in the school's shared notebook about where you were on Tuesday, and every particle in them is right. The teacher who reads it says it is perfectly clear and slightly odd, and cannot immediately say why. Nothing is wrong. The pieces are in an order nobody would choose.
setting.jp: 昨日、図書館で本を読みました。
setting.en: Time, place, object, verb — the neutral order.

extensions.scene: You rewrite the second sentence into the default running order and it stops sounding translated, without a single word being added or removed. The particles were carrying the meaning all along; what the order was carrying was the ease.
extensions.jp: 月曜日、公園で友達に会いました。
extensions.en: Monday, at the park, met a friend.

extensions.t: Exactly one thing cannot move: the verb stays last. Everything else negotiates, and moving a piece earlier gives it emphasis rather than breaking anything. That is why particles carry so much weight here — English uses position to show who did what to whom, and Japanese has spent that budget elsewhere.
extensions.scene: You try putting the place first instead, to stress it, and the sentence survives intact — because the particle sitting on it says what that piece is doing regardless of where in the line it happens to stand.
extensions.jp: 図書館で昨日本を読みました。
extensions.en: Same sentence, place fronted for emphasis — still fine.

flags: No factual claims — an ordinary situation.

items.step: Step 4 · Verbs: from dictionary form up

setting.scene: A group chat with three other teachers, set up on your second day, which is where the actual information about the school lives — what time the gate is locked, whose turn it is on Saturday. You have been answering in full polite sentences and it reads like a letter from a bank. Everyone else is writing in the shortest form there is.
setting.jp: 明日学校へ行く。
setting.en: I'll go to school tomorrow. (casual)

extensions.scene: Somebody asks what time you eat, meaning whether you will be in the staffroom at noon, and the answer is the same bare form — it is not shorthand or laziness, it is the shape a dictionary would list and the shape everything else is built from.
extensions.jp: 十二時に食べる。
extensions.en: I eat at twelve.

extensions.scene: You use the same form in an email to the teacher who runs your section, and it arrives like answering a work message with 'yeah, going'. Nothing was ungrammatical. The register was two floors below the room.
extensions.jp: 明日、学校へ行きます。
extensions.en: Same sentence, polite — です・ます for anyone but friends.

flags: No factual claims — an ordinary situation.

items.step: Step 4 · Verbs: from dictionary form up

setting.scene: The first parents' evening, and you have twelve conversations to get through with people you have never met, about children you have known for three weeks. Whatever else you get wrong tonight, the ending on every verb should be the same one — the safe adult default, the form that is never wrong with a stranger.
setting.jp: 毎日勉強します。
setting.en: He studies every day.

extensions.scene: A parent asks what time you get in and you answer about yourself for the first time all evening. Same ending, your own verb, and the tense is sitting inside it rather than being added on afterwards.
extensions.jp: 毎日七時に起きます。
extensions.en: I get up at seven every day.

extensions.scene: How a verb reaches this ending depends on which family it belongs to, and you have been guessing all evening — mostly correctly, which is worse, because you have no idea why. The next lesson sorts every verb you will meet.
extensions.jp: 食べます。飲みます。します。
extensions.en: Three families, three routes to the same ending.

flags: No factual claims — an ordinary situation.

items.step: Step 4 · Verbs: from dictionary form up

setting.scene: You have started keeping verbs in a notebook and the list has stopped being useful, because it is alphabetical and the language does not care about that. Every verb you meet belongs to one of two families, the family decides how it bends, and telling them apart is a two-second test you can run on sight.
setting.jp: 食べる → 食べます
setting.en: Ichi: drop る, add ます.

extensions.scene: You re-sort the notebook into two columns and the test does most of the work by itself: if it does not end in る it is the other family, guaranteed, no exceptions to worry about.
extensions.jp: 行く → 行きます
extensions.en: Go: the last sound shifts to the い row.

extensions.t: A handful end in いる or える and are Go anyway: 帰る, 入る, 走る, 切る, 知る. They are common enough to be worth learning as a set today rather than meeting one at a time in the middle of a sentence.
extensions.scene: Two verbs you use daily — going home and going in — fail the test. They look like one family and belong to the other, and there are five of them worth memorising as a block.
extensions.jp: 帰る → 帰ります
extensions.en: Looks Ichi, is Go — 帰ります, not 帰る→帰ます.

flags: No factual claims — an ordinary situation.

items.step: Step 4 · Verbs: from dictionary form up

setting.scene: Your vocabulary list has forty two-kanji nouns on it and you have been learning them as nouns. Somebody points out that most of them are also verbs — that one small word turns almost any of them into something you can do — and the list quietly doubles in value without a single new entry.
setting.jp: 毎日、日本語を勉強します。
setting.en: I study Japanese every day.

extensions.scene: You try it on a noun nobody taught you as a verb and it works, which is the point: the pattern is productive, so every word of that shape you learn from now on arrives with a verb attached.
extensions.jp: 毎日、散歩します。
extensions.en: I take a walk every day.

extensions.t: The sorting test from the last lesson does not apply to these, and trying to apply it is the classic accident: 勉強する is neither family, so 勉強しります and 勉強しる are both wrong. It and 来る are simply irregular, and they are the two most common verbs in the language.
extensions.scene: You run the two-column test on it out of habit and get an answer that does not exist. These two verbs sit outside the system entirely, and there are only two of them.
extensions.jp: 来ます。します。
extensions.en: The two irregulars — learned whole, not sorted.

flags: No factual claims — an ordinary situation.
散歩 arrives properly in Step 7; used here as a familiar noun+する.

items.step: Step 4 · Verbs: from dictionary form up

setting.scene: Saturday, and three of the teachers have taken you to a ramen place near the station, which is the first time all month anybody has spoken to you at normal speed. Every sentence at the table ends in a sound you half recognise and cannot produce, and all of them are about what happened last night.
setting.jp: 昨日、ラーメンを食べた。
setting.en: I ate ramen yesterday. (casual)

extensions.scene: Somebody asks whether you went to the festival and you answer in the same register for the first time — the plain past, at a table where nobody is anybody's teacher for the evening.
extensions.jp: 行った。
extensions.en: I went.

extensions.scene: The shape is not new. It is built exactly like the connector form coming in two lessons, with one sound swapped at the end, so learning either of them hands you the other for nothing.
extensions.jp: 飲んで / 飲んだ
extensions.en: Same machinery, one sound apart.

flags: No factual claims — an ordinary situation.
ラーメン is katakana and unlisted; it appears in the module's own example.

items.step: Step 4 · Verbs: from dictionary form up

setting.scene: Monday morning, and the section head asks what you did at the weekend — the same question the table asked on Saturday night, in a room where the answer cannot possibly be the same shape. Same event, same verb, same week, and one whole floor up in politeness because of who is standing in front of you.
setting.jp: 昨日映画を見ました。
setting.en: I watched a film yesterday.

extensions.scene: She asks whether you have eaten, meaning this morning, and the negative version of the same tense arrives by exactly the same route — nothing new to learn and nothing to sort, just one piece swapped at the end of the word.
extensions.jp: 朝ごはんを食べませんでした。
extensions.en: I didn't eat breakfast.

extensions.scene: You reach for the plain past you learned on Saturday and try to make it polite by adding to the end of it, which produces something that is not a word. This form is built from the ます stem, and it ignores the sound-change chart entirely.
extensions.jp: 飲みました。
extensions.en: Not 飲んだました — built from the stem, not the plain past.

flags: No factual claims — an ordinary situation.

items.step: Step 4 · Verbs: from dictionary form up

setting.scene: The morning routine you have to describe for the school's health form is four actions long and you can say all four of them separately. What you cannot do is join them, so the answer reads like a telegram. This one form is the connector every later pattern plugs into, and it is the hardest conjugation in the whole stage.
setting.jp: 朝起きて、顔を洗います。
setting.en: I get up and wash my face.

extensions.scene: You chain the rest of it yourself and the whole morning arrives as a single sentence rather than four. Only the last verb carries the tense for any of it; everything in front is simply hooked on and takes whatever that final verb decides.
extensions.jp: 朝ごはんを食べて、学校へ行きます。
extensions.en: I eat breakfast and go to school.

extensions.scene: Which sound the form takes depends on the verb's last kana, and the chart has six rows and one outright liar in it — the verb for going, which does not behave like the row it belongs to.
extensions.jp: 行って
extensions.en: 行く breaks its own row — 行いて is wrong.

flags: No factual claims — an ordinary situation.
顔 and 洗う sit outside the Step 4 bank; both are in the module's own example.

items.step: Step 4 · Verbs: from dictionary form up

setting.scene: A phone call from the school office at ten past eight, asking where you are, and the honest answer is on a platform two stations away watching a delay board. What the question wants is not what you did or what you will do but what is happening at this exact moment, which needs a form English builds with is and Japanese builds onto the verb.
setting.jp: 今、雨が降っています。
setting.en: It's raining now.

extensions.scene: She asks what you can see from where you are standing, and you describe the platform — the same shape, this time in your own sentence, with everything in it happening at the moment you say it.
extensions.jp: 今、電車を待っています。
extensions.en: I'm waiting for the train now.

extensions.scene: You use it about where you live and it comes out meaning something you did not intend — because this form has a second life, and the next lesson is entirely about the difference.
extensions.jp: 東京に住んでいます。
extensions.en: I live in Tokyo — not 'in the middle of living'.

flags: No factual claims — an ordinary situation.
待つ is Step 5 bank; used one step early in a natural sentence.

items.step: Step 4 · Verbs: from dictionary form up

setting.scene: New class, first lesson, and thirty-four children want to know everything about you at once — where you live, whether you are married, whether you have a dog. All three answers describe a state you are in now, and every one of them got there because something happened in the past and then stopped changing.
setting.jp: 東京に住んでいます。
setting.en: I live in Tokyo.

extensions.scene: They ask about the teacher who left, and the same form describes where she is now — a result that is still standing, not an action anybody is in the middle of.
extensions.jp: 国に帰っています。
extensions.en: She's gone back to her country (and is there).

extensions.scene: You answer the where-do-you-live question with the plain polite form instead, and it lands as a plan rather than a fact — as though you were describing a move you have not made yet.
extensions.jp: 東京に住んでいます。
extensions.en: 住みます would sound like a moving plan, not a life.

flags: No factual claims — an ordinary situation.

items.step: Step 4 · Verbs: from dictionary form up

setting.scene: You come back to the staffroom after lunch and the window is open. It was shut when you left. Nobody is standing near it and nobody is going to be blamed. What you want to say is a description of the room, not a report of anyone's action — and English hands you one verb for both jobs with no warning that a choice is being made.
setting.jp: 窓が開いています。
setting.en: The window is open.

extensions.scene: You close it, and now there is a person in the sentence — you — which means the other twin of the same verb, and the particle changes to match without you touching it.
extensions.jp: 窓を閉めました。
extensions.en: I closed the window.

extensions.t: The self-check that catches it: if you find を sitting in front of an it-just-happens verb, one of the two is wrong. 窓を閉まりました is wrong twice — 閉まる cannot take を, and a person closing something needs 閉めました.
extensions.scene: You write it in the shared notebook with the wrong twin and the wrong particle, and the sentence is broken in two places at once, neither of which English would have flagged.
extensions.jp: 窓が閉まりました。
extensions.en: The window closed — no one did it, so が and the happen-twin.

flags: No factual claims — an ordinary situation.

items.step: Step 4 · Verbs: from dictionary form up

setting.scene: Half past twelve and the section head is doing the rounds before the afternoon meeting, checking who still needs to eat, who has sent the forms in, who has done the thing they said they would do at nine. Every question she asks is about whether something is finished, and every answer is one word plus a past tense.
setting.jp: もう昼ごはんを食べました。
setting.en: I've already eaten lunch.

extensions.scene: You ask her the same about the paperwork you handed in on Friday, because nobody has said anything since and the deadline was yesterday. Same word, your question, checking a door is shut.
extensions.jp: もう見ましたか。
extensions.en: Have you already looked at it?

extensions.scene: Its mirror turns up in the next answer down the row — somebody has not eaten, and the not-yet version pairs with a different ending entirely. The two words are one system: door closed, door still open.
extensions.jp: まだ食べていません。
extensions.en: Not yet — まだ pairs with ていません.

flags: No factual claims — an ordinary situation.

items.step: Step 4 · Verbs: from dictionary form up

setting.scene: The medical for the job is at two and the instruction sheet said nothing after midnight. At half past one somebody offers you a biscuit and you have to explain, in a staffroom, that you have not eaten — not that you did not eat, which is a different sentence and closes a door that is still very much open.
setting.jp: まだ食べていません。
setting.en: I haven't eaten yet.

extensions.scene: At the clinic the nurse asks whether the forms came back from the school and you use the same shape about somebody else's outstanding job — still open, still expected, not yet done.
extensions.jp: まだ来ていません。
extensions.en: It hasn't come yet.

extensions.scene: You say it with the ordinary polite past instead and it reports that eating simply did not happen — historical, finished, nothing pending. Not-yet-ness is a present state and it needs the present-state form.
extensions.jp: まだ食べていません。
extensions.en: Not まだ食べませんでした — that closes the door.

flags: No factual claims — an ordinary situation.

items.step: Step 4 · Verbs: from dictionary form up

setting.scene: You spend twenty minutes hunting for the future tense, because the school calendar for next term needs describing and every sentence you want is about something that has not happened yet. There is nothing to find. The form you already have covers habits, plans, promises and scheduled events without changing shape.
setting.jp: 毎日コーヒーを飲みます。
setting.en: I drink coffee every day. (habit)

extensions.scene: You write the line about next Monday with the identical ending you used for the habit, and nothing whatever marks it as future except the word for Monday sitting at the front. If you know it is happening, the non-past says so.
extensions.jp: 月曜日に行きます。
extensions.en: I'm going on Monday.

extensions.t: The instinct to hunt for a future marker produces things like 行くでしょう where a plain 行きます was wanted. でしょう is a guess, not a tense — reaching for it to mean 'will' quietly downgrades a fact into a probably.
extensions.scene: You add a word you half-remember meaning will, and the sentence stops being a plan and becomes a forecast — which is not what a calendar means at all, and quietly downgrades something you know into something you suspect.
extensions.jp: 明日、行きます。
extensions.en: Not 行くでしょう — that's 'probably', not 'will'.

flags: No factual claims — an ordinary situation.

items.step: Step 4 · Verbs: from dictionary form up

setting.scene: Two conversations, four minutes apart, in the same room. One with the teacher you eat lunch with every day; one with the section head who signs your leave. The words are nearly identical and the endings cannot be, and the level tracks your relationship with the person rather than the subject or your mood.
setting.jp: 先生、明日は休みます。
setting.en: To a teacher: polite.

extensions.scene: You say the same thing to the friend at the next desk on your way out and drop a whole floor without thinking about it, which is exactly right — the dial moved because the listener moved, not because the news did.
extensions.jp: 明日、休む。
extensions.en: Same news, to a friend.

extensions.t: The classic error is not picking the wrong level. It is drifting between them inside one conversation, which reads as unstable rather than casual — pick a level per listener at the start and hold it to the end.
extensions.scene: Halfway through a longer conversation with the section head you relax, and a single plain verb slips in among the polite ones. Nobody says anything about it and nobody needs to. Everybody in the room heard it happen.
extensions.jp: 休みます。
extensions.en: Hold the level you started on.

flags: No factual claims — an ordinary situation.

items.step: Step 4 · Verbs: from dictionary form up

setting.scene: The end-of-term report wants a sentence about the children who joined late, and you cannot build it — every version needs a joining word that does not exist. Japanese puts the whole description in front of the noun with nothing between them, and this is the single structure that turns short sentences into real ones.
setting.jp: 離婚した人は、もう一度結婚しますか。
setting.en: Do people who have divorced marry again?

extensions.scene: You write your own line about the class and the clause slots in front of the noun with no connector at all — no who, no that, nothing to translate, which is exactly why it feels wrong for the first month.
extensions.jp: 昨日来た学生は日本人です。
extensions.en: The student who came yesterday is Japanese.

extensions.t: Three specific errors. Never です or ます inside the clause — 離婚しました人 is wrong, it is 離婚した人. Never insert a joining word, because there is no equivalent of who or that. And never add の, which is for joining nouns, not clauses.
extensions.scene: Your first attempt is polite inside the clause, which nothing in English would warn you about, and the politeness belongs at the very end of the sentence rather than in the middle of it.
extensions.jp: 昨日来た学生です。
extensions.en: Not 昨日来ました学生 — politeness waits for the end.

flags: No factual claims — an ordinary situation.
離婚/結婚 sit well outside Step 4 vocabulary; they are the module's own example sentence, kept for fidelity.

setting.scene: The bank again, and the account has hit a problem that needs the teller to fetch somebody. She asks you to sit down, and then you need to ask her something back — the neutral polite request, the one that works on counters, taxi drivers and teachers, and the only one you have.
setting.jp: ちょっと待ってください。
setting.en: Please wait a moment.

extensions.scene: The form has to go to the school for a stamp and back here by Friday, so you ask the office to look at it today rather than tomorrow. Your request this time, same shape, on a verb of your own.
extensions.jp: 今日、見てください。
extensions.en: Please look at it today.

extensions.scene: The answer side is part of the pattern and it is not always a word for yes. いいですよ and どうぞ are both agreement — and a hesitant ちょっと with nothing after it is very often the whole answer.
extensions.jp: ちょっと…
extensions.en: A no wearing softness — take the hesitation as the answer.

flags: No factual claims — an ordinary situation.

setting.scene: A school trip to a temple, thirty-four children, and a member of staff comes over to you rather than to them — which means whatever is about to be said is for you to pass on. Inside the hall, no photographs. It is a request rather than a rule on a sign, and the form matches that.
setting.jp: ここで写真を撮らないでください。
setting.en: Please don't take photos here.

extensions.scene: You turn round and say it to the class, and then say a gentler one to the child who has been worrying all morning about getting something wrong — the same shape, doing comfort rather than instruction.
extensions.jp: 心配しないでください。
extensions.en: Please don't worry.

extensions.scene: On the way out there is a sign that means the same thing in a completely different voice: not a person asking this person now, but a standing rule that was true before you arrived.
extensions.jp: ここでたばこを吸ってはいけません。
extensions.en: No smoking here — a rule, not a request.

flags: No factual claims — an ordinary situation.
心配 uses kanji outside KANJI_DICT — furigana needed. Kept because 心配しないでください is the module's own example and the most useful sentence in the lesson.

setting.scene: The staffroom has assigned desks and one spare, and you have been standing with a laptop for four minutes because nobody has told you whether the spare is spare. Japanese social space runs on asking first, and this is the asking — before you sit, borrow, photograph, or leave early.
setting.jp: ここに座ってもいいですか。
setting.en: May I sit here?

extensions.scene: Later you need the good stapler off somebody else's desk, and the same question does it — asking before taking is not deference here, it is the ordinary running order.
extensions.jp: 使ってもいいですか。
extensions.en: May I use it?

extensions.scene: Reading the answer is half the skill. どうぞ is yes and needs no words around it. あ、ちょっと… is a no wearing softness, and pressing past it makes things worse in both directions at once.
extensions.jp: あ、ちょっと…
extensions.en: That's the no. Don't ask twice.

flags: No factual claims — an ordinary situation.

setting.scene: The pool, the first hot week, and the rules are on a board by the gate in language that does not soften anything. Some of it is pictures. Most of it is one pattern, repeated, which is the pattern signage uses when the rule was true before you arrived and will be true after you leave.
setting.jp: ここでたばこを吸ってはいけません。
setting.en: You must not smoke here.

extensions.scene: You have to put it into English for the class and then back into Japanese for the parent who arrives late, and it is the same flat shape both times — no room in it and none intended.
extensions.jp: ここに入ってはいけません。
extensions.en: You must not go in here.

extensions.scene: You use it on a child who is about to do something harmless and it lands far heavier than you meant. To stop a person, rather than state a rule, the gentler request form is the right tool.
extensions.jp: 入らないでください。
extensions.en: Please don't go in — asking a person, not quoting a rule.

flags: No factual claims — an ordinary situation.

setting.scene: The clinic sends you home with a week of tablets and an instruction that is not a suggestion, and the pharmacist writes it into the booklet you now carry. Every day, whether or not you feel any better. The sentence for a duty like that is built out of pieces you already own, assembled in a shape English does not have.
setting.jp: 毎日薬を飲まなければなりません。
setting.en: I have to take medicine every day.

extensions.scene: Six o'clock, and you are the first to leave a room where nobody has moved — so you say why, and this is the polite exit as much as it is an obligation.
extensions.jp: もう帰らなければなりません。
extensions.en: I have to go now.

extensions.scene: Taken apart, the sentence says that if you do not drink it, it will not do. There is no direct word for must anywhere in it — the obligation is built by ruling out the not-doing, which is why the shape looks so long for so small an idea.
extensions.jp: 飲まなければなりません。
extensions.en: Literally: if I don't drink it, it won't do.

claims: Prescriptions are dispensed by a pharmacy rather than the clinic, and recorded in a patient-held booklet

setting.scene: Saturday practice is optional this month and one family has spent four minutes apologising for something they do not need to apologise for. You have one sentence in which to release them, and the sentence that forbids them is built from entirely different parts — but English builds both out of the same words, so the instinct is to negate must and hope.
setting.jp: 明日は来なくてもいいです。
setting.en: You don't have to come tomorrow.

extensions.scene: A colleague asks whether she has to fill in the second form as well, and you get to be the one giving mercy — same shape, answering a must-I question with a no that grants rather than forbids.
extensions.jp: 書かなくてもいいです。
extensions.en: You don't have to write it.

extensions.scene: Say the other one by mistake and you have banned a child from the school on Saturday. Both sentences are perfectly grammatical and nothing warns you that the message inverted.
extensions.jp: 来てはいけません。
extensions.en: You must NOT come — a different sentence entirely.

flags: No factual claims — an ordinary situation.

setting.scene: Three sentences from this step form a triangle, and one corner of it is where English speakers do real damage. Must do, must not do, and do not have to do — the first two feel like opposites and the third feels like a negative of the first, which is exactly the wiring that sends a family home thinking their son is banned.
setting.jp: 来なくてもいいです。
setting.en: You don't have to come.

extensions.scene: You draw the triangle out on paper for yourself, and the two dangerous corners share no material at all: one is the negative form plus permission, the other is the connector form plus prohibition. Nothing about them overlaps.
extensions.jp: 来てはいけません。
extensions.en: You must not come — different parts, opposite meaning.

extensions.t: The must corner itself is modular: なければ, ないと or なきゃ on the left; なりません, いけません or だめ on the right. Most combinations work and mean the same thing, so learn two slots rather than six patterns — and note the double negative is doing the work in all of them, which is why adding your own extra negative is the one honestly wrong move.
extensions.scene: You hear four different versions of the same obligation in one week and assume they are four patterns. They are two slots with three fillings each, and every combination means what you think it means.
extensions.jp: 行かないといけない。
extensions.en: Same meaning, lighter register — two slots, swapped.

flags: No factual claims — an ordinary situation.

setting.scene: Six o'clock, the last two people in the staffroom, and both of you have been finding small things to do for twenty minutes. The decision is essentially already made and somebody has to say it out loud. This form does not ask — it moves a group that has already agreed.
setting.jp: 一緒に帰りましょう。
setting.en: Let's go home together.

extensions.scene: At the station you both look at the same shop at the same moment, which is agreement enough on its own — so the sentence skips the asking entirely and goes straight to the deciding, which is what this form is for.
extensions.jp: お茶を飲みましょう。
extensions.en: Let's have some tea.

extensions.scene: You use it on somebody you have known for four days and it assumes rather more than you have. For a genuine invitation, one that leaves the other person somewhere to stand, there is a softer opener two lessons away.
extensions.jp: 一緒に帰りませんか。
extensions.en: Won't you go home together? — leaves room to decline.

flags: No factual claims — an ordinary situation.

setting.scene: The teacher across the desk is carrying a box of textbooks with her chin on top of it and has said nothing, because saying something would be asking. You are not deciding anything jointly here — you are offering, which is the same form with one syllable added and a completely different social job.
setting.jp: 手伝いましょうか。
setting.en: Shall I help you?

extensions.scene: Later it is genuinely joint — the two of you are standing in front of a window nobody has opened all afternoon, and the question is what to do rather than whether you will do it for her.
extensions.jp: 窓を開けましょうか。
extensions.en: Shall we open the window?

extensions.t: Learn the replies with the offer. お願いします accepts gratefully; 大丈夫です declines politely — the same 大丈夫 from the convenience store lesson, doing the same work. And the か is load-bearing: 手伝いますか asks whether you help in general, which is a different question.
extensions.scene: She answers with two words and you have to know which of them was a yes. One hands you the box; the other means she has it, thank you, and neither contains a no.
extensions.jp: 大丈夫です。
extensions.en: I'm fine, thanks — a polite decline, not a yes.

flags: No factual claims — an ordinary situation.

setting.scene: A month in. The teacher at the next desk has stayed late twice this week and you would like to suggest lunch, without putting her in the position of turning you down to your face — which she would find harder than you would. The negative question builds the exit into the grammar.
setting.jp: 一緒に昼ごはんを食べませんか。
setting.en: Won't you have lunch with me?

extensions.scene: It goes well enough that you try a second one for the weekend, aimed slightly upward — at somebody senior, where the room to decline matters more rather than less.
extensions.jp: 一緒に映画を見ませんか。
extensions.en: Won't you come and see a film?

extensions.scene: The answer is not はい or いいえ. Acceptance comes as いいですね or ぜひ; the refusal comes as ちょっと, trailing off into nothing, and the trailing off is the entire message.
extensions.jp: いいですね。
extensions.en: That'd be nice — the acceptance, where a bare はい would be odd.

flags: No factual claims — an ordinary situation.

setting.scene: The end-of-year form asks where you would like to be placed next April, and it is the first document since you arrived that has asked what you want rather than what you are. Your own wishes, stated flat, in a form that belongs to you and only to you.
setting.jp: 日本へ行きたいです。
setting.en: I want to go to Japan.

extensions.scene: Somebody asks over lunch what you want to eat, which is this same form pointed at you between equals — and answering it is the easiest complete sentence you have built all week, because it is about the one mind you have access to.
extensions.jp: お茶を飲みたいです。
extensions.en: I want some tea.

extensions.scene: You use it about your sister, who has been talking about visiting for months, and the sentence claims to know something you cannot know. Japanese marks other people's insides differently, and the machinery for it arrives in Stage 2.
extensions.jp: 妹は行きたがっています。
extensions.en: My sister wants to go — read from outside, not claimed.

flags: No factual claims — an ordinary situation.
行きたがっている is Stage 2 grammar, shown here only as the correct alternative.

setting.scene: The apartment came with a fridge, a light and nothing else, and four weeks in you have a list on the back of an envelope. Somebody at work asks what you still need, and the answer is about things rather than actions — which Japanese splits into two different words where English uses one.
setting.jp: 新しいかばんがほしいです。
setting.en: I want a new bag.

extensions.scene: Your birthday is in three weeks and the interrogation has started early. Same word, same particle — and the particle is the thing to watch, because the thing you want is not something you are doing anything to.
extensions.jp: 車がほしいです。
extensions.en: I want a car.

extensions.scene: Half your list is not things at all but things you want to do, and those need the other form entirely. A new bag wants one word; buying the bag wants the other.
extensions.jp: かばんを買いたいです。
extensions.en: I want to buy a bag — actions take たい.

flags: No factual claims — an ordinary situation.

setting.scene: Leave has to go in by the end of the month and the section head is asking everyone in turn what they are doing in August. Two of your colleagues answer with something vague. Yours is not vague — the flights are booked — and there is a form for a plan you have actually committed to.
setting.jp: 夏に国へ帰るつもりです。
